analysis.investment_thesis: Gabriel India is a genuinely good business (ROCE 28.4%) but trades at an egregious valuation — Earnings Yield of only ~2.7% (EBIT INR 390 Cr / EV ~INR 14,602 Cr) — far below the 12% minimum the Magic Formula demands. The Magic Formula requires BOTH metrics to be high; with only one firing, this is a pass.
key_strengths: ROCE of 28.4% — above the 25% 'excellent' threshold; sustained and expanding over 3+ years
Revenue CAGR 20.6% and net profit CAGR 39.9% over FY22-25 — genuine operating momentum
Near-zero leverage (D/E 0.08), clean balance sheet, OCF positive all 4 years
key_risks: Earnings Yield of ~2.7% (EBIT/EV) — five-to-six times below Magic Formula's minimum; priced for perfection at 56x P/E and 34.5x EV/EBITDA
FCF collapsed to zero in FY25 (Operating CF INR 204 Cr minus Capex INR 209 Cr) — capex is consuming all cash generation and accelerating (76→89→163→209 Cr over 4 years)
Thin operating margin of 6.91% typical of OEM auto-parts suppliers — leaves little room for error in a cyclical industry tied to auto volumes
red_flags: Earnings Yield ~2.7% vs. Magic Formula minimum of 12% — stock is ~4-5x overpriced on this metric
FY25 Free Cash Flow = INR 0 Cr despite INR 245 Cr reported net profit — FCF conversion is near-zero
Capex growing 175% in 3 years (INR 76 Cr → INR 209 Cr) with no corresponding jump in FCF — capital intensity is rising, not falling
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Gabriel India: Earnings Yield = EBIT INR 390 Cr / EV ~INR 14,602 Cr (Market Cap 14,571 + Debt 69 - Cash 38) = **2.67%**. That is catastrophically low — my framework requires >12% to be interesting and >15% to be exciting. Return on Capital (using ROCE proxy) is a strong 28.4%, which is genuinely excellent and reflects real competitive strength in shock absorbers/suspension for OEMs. But Magic Formula is AND logic, not OR logic — both metrics must rank well. Here, one is top-decile and the other is bottom-decile.

The FCF story makes the valuation even harder to justify. Despite INR 245 Cr in net profit, FY25 FCF was effectively INR 0 (OCF 204 Cr minus Capex 209 Cr). Capex is tripling in four years as Gabriel chases capacity for EVs and railways — a real growth story, but the market is already pricing it in at 56x earnings. At this valuation the investor is lending the company money to grow and receiving very little earnings yield in return. The business may well be worth holding if purchased at 15-20x earnings; at 56x, the Magic Formula says walk away.
